claims.text: High-temperature oxidation resistance in multiprincipal-element alloys is governed by the ability to form a continuous, adherent protective oxide scale.
Cr2O3 and Al2O3 are examples of protective oxides that can improve oxidation resistance.
Material integrity during high-temperature exposure is governed by formation of the protective oxide scale.
Insufficient Cr or Al concentration disrupts formation of a continuous protective oxide.
Absence of a Cr2O3 layer can cause further outward diffusion of Mn.
Outward diffusion of Mn following failure of Cr2O3 formation leads to Mn3O4 formation.
Mn-rich oxides formed after protective-scale failure are more porous and less protective.
Formation of a stable, adherent oxide barrier minimizes interdiffusion and further oxidation.
Poor oxide-scale adherence can promote breakaway oxidation.
Volatile V-rich oxides can deteriorate scale adherence at temperatures of at least 700 °C.
The proposed governing behavior applies throughout approximately 700–950 °C in air.
The 700–950 °C range is relevant to fusion plasma-facing components and other harsh-environment applications.
Increasing protective-element content is predicted to produce a more coherent and adherent oxide scale than a lower-Cr/Al baseline.
Increasing protective-element content is predicted to reduce oxidation rates relative to the lower-Cr/Al baseline.
Increasing protective-element content is predicted to improve post-oxidation mechanical integrity.
A protective-element-deficient baseline is predicted to develop a thicker oxide scale and undergo accelerated degradation.
The controlled comparison varies Cr or Al content between otherwise similar multiprincipal-element alloy samples.
The comparison exposes both sample sets to air at 950 °C and characterizes oxide phases, morphology, mass gain, and post-oxidation mechanical properties.
XRD, SEM, TGA, and tensile or creep testing provide measurable readouts of oxide identity, scale morphology, oxidation kinetics, and mechanical integrity.
Failure of the high-protective-element alloy to show a more coherent and adherent scale, lower oxidation rate, or improved mechanical integrity relative to the control would falsify the hypothesis.
